questions.question_text: Where are the legal and regulatory requirements that apply to your use or building of AI kept, and how do the people they apply to learn of them and of changes (for example onboarding, training, announcements)?
How does your organisation keep track of new or changing laws and regulations that affect its AI? Who decides what must change in how AI is used or built?

Where is your AI risk management policy kept, and how do the people it applies to (staff, developers, vendors' account owners) come to know it and any changes to it, for example through onboarding, training, acknowledgement or announcements?
How do your AI rules apply to AI that others built or sold to you, as well as AI you run yourself, so that it meets your existing legal obligations and risk controls? Who checks this?

What do your procedures require to happen before an AI system goes live and while it is in use (testing and validation, legal and risk review, ongoing monitoring), and what record shows these steps were followed for a recent AI system?
How do your AI policies and procedures address qualities such as safety, security, fairness, explainability and privacy for your AI systems, and where can we see this applied to a recent AI system?
How do your rules for building and training your own models set standards for data quality and model training? Where can we see them applied to your latest model?
How do you decide how much risk assessment and oversight an AI system needs before it is used, for example using a risk rating of its possible impact and likelihood? Who makes that decision?
How are your AI systems placed on one common risk scale? How often is that rating revisited as the system or its use changes?
What information do you record about each AI system, for example its purpose, limits, known risks and test results? Where are these records kept?
How often do you check whether your AI risk management process is working? Who is responsible for acting on what the check finds?
How do you decide what to tell customers, regulators or the public about your use of AI and its risks, and who approves what is shared?
Where are your AI risk management policies and procedures kept, and how do the people they apply to come to know them and their changes (for example onboarding, training, announcements)?
How are your AI systems monitored after they go live for performance, bias and security problems? What record shows the latest results?
Where is your procedure for handling AI incidents kept, and how do the people involved come to know it and its changes (for example training, drills, announcements)?
Which roles or teams are responsible for monitoring your AI and responding to AI incidents, and where is that assignment written down?
How often do you review the results of your AI monitoring and incidents to decide whether your AI risk management needs to change? Who carries out the review?
In the 'AI systems' sheet, list each AI system your organisation uses or builds, with what it involves and the worst realistic outcome if it gets things wrong.
How does a new or changed AI system get added to your AI system inventory, and who is responsible for that?
How does an AI system's criticality decide how much goes into its inventory entry — which details are recorded and how often it is reviewed — and where is that shown?
When an AI system is retired or replaced, how do you carry it out safely, for example moving to the replacement and checking what depends on it? Who signs it off?
What happens to the models, data and records of a retired AI system, and for how long are they kept?
Where is your procedure for retiring AI systems kept, and how do the people it applies to come to know it and its changes (for example onboarding, training, announcements)?

Who is responsible for AI risk in your organisation, from senior management to the teams that buy, build, test and run AI, and where are these responsibilities written down? How do people learn who to go to?
How do the people involved in AI risk talk to each other and raise concerns, for example regular meetings or an escalation route? What record shows it happening?
How do you keep the people who check or approve an AI system independent of the people who built or bought it? Where are conflicts of interest declared or recorded?
What AI risk training do your staff and partners get, for example on laws, AI policies and possible harms? How does it differ for technical and oversight roles?
How do staff acknowledge their AI responsibilities and learn of significant changes to AI systems or policies?
Who do staff and partners escalate AI risk concerns to, and how do they know that route?
How does executive leadership decide how much AI risk the organisation will accept? Where is that decision recorded?
How often does leadership or a board committee review AI risks and approve decisions on high-risk AI use? What record, such as minutes or a report, shows this?
How do you make sure the people who decide on AI risks bring different disciplines and backgrounds, for example legal, security, business and technical staff? Where is who took part recorded?
When your organisation lacks expertise on AI risk, how do you bring in outside help? Who decides when it is needed?
Where are the roles and responsibilities of the people who use, oversee or monitor your AI systems written down, and how do those people come to know them and any changes?
How do you train and check the skills of the people who operate or oversee your AI systems? Who owns this?
How are problems in the way people work with AI, such as over-reliance on its answers or confusing screens, captured and tracked? Where are they recorded?
At what point in an AI project do legal, compliance and risk staff get involved, and what shows they were (for example a sign-off or review record)?
How are decisions to build or deploy AI challenged before they go ahead, for example by an independent review, audit or red-teaming? Who carries out the challenge?
How can staff raise a concern about an AI system without fear of reprisal? Where are concerns recorded?
How do you assess the potential harm of an AI system before it is used and again when it changes? Who carries out the assessment?
Where are the results of these assessments recorded, and how are they used in your wider view of AI risk?
How are the impacts you have assessed for your AI systems shared beyond the team, for example with leadership, affected users or customers? Who decides what is shared?
How are your AI systems tested before and during use? Where are the results kept?
Where are the steps for reporting and handling an AI incident kept, and how do staff come to know them and any changes?
How do you share what you learn about the limits of your AI systems and about incidents, inside the organisation and with outside parties where needed? Who decides what is shared?
How do you collect feedback about your AI from people outside the team that runs it, such as users, customers or people affected by it? Where is it recorded?
How is outside feedback about your AI reviewed and prioritised, and who decides what is changed as a result?
Who is given the chance to give feedback on how an AI system is designed or set up (for example the people who build, run, use or oversee it), and how is that feedback gathered?
When feedback on an AI system is received, how is it weighed and accepted or rejected before anything changes? Who decides?
How does feedback from the people who use or are affected by an AI system lead to changes in how it is designed or run? Can you give a recent example?

Where are your rules for using third-party AI (models, AI services and the data they rely on) kept, and how do the people they apply to come to know them and any changes, for example through onboarding, training or announcements?

Before your organisation starts using a third-party AI system or data source, how is it checked for what it does, what it was trained on and its known limits, for example through vendor documentation and your own testing? Who signs off?

How do you check that third-party AI and the data it was built on do not infringe someone else's intellectual property or other rights, for example through contract terms or licence reviews? Where is the outcome recorded?
How are your rules for third-party AI reviewed and updated, for example after a vendor change, an incident or a new law? Who owns that review?
How do you choose, check and keep watching the existing model your own model is built on, for example its source, licence and known weaknesses? Who owns this?
How does your incident response plan cover a failure or incident in a third-party AI service or data source you rely on? Who owns that part of the plan?
For the third-party AI services you cannot do without, what backup exists (for example another provider or a manual process)? Who decided it was enough?
How does your organisation record what each AI system it uses or builds is for, in light of its mission and goals? Who owns that record?
When the purpose of an AI system is reviewed, how are the organisation's stated principles and the values of the people affected taken into account, and where is the outcome recorded?
How does your organisation decide how much risk it will accept from AI, for example by type of harm and by level of impact? Where are these limits recorded?

What happens when an AI system goes beyond the risk your organisation is willing to accept, or is used for a purpose it was not approved for? Can you give a recent example and the record of the decision?
How does your organisation decide what skills and training people need before they operate AI systems? Where are the training records kept?
How do you tell the people who use your AI systems what the systems can and cannot do, and what is out of bounds? Where do they find this information?
How does your organisation choose which AI risks to measure first? Where are the chosen measures recorded?
How are AI risks you decided not to measure, or cannot yet measure, recorded, and who accepted that decision?
What happens when an AI system performs beyond the acceptable limits you have set for it, for example on error rates? Where is the decision recorded?
How often does your organisation check whether its AI measures and controls still work? Who does it?
When errors, incidents or harm from AI are reported, how are they recorded and used to change the measures or controls? Can you show a recent example?
How does your organisation track AI risks that appear after an AI system is in use, including ones nobody expected? Where is this recorded?
How is feedback from users and affected people about AI compared with your own measures of how the AI performs? Where is the comparison recorded?

For AI risks that are hard to measure, how does your organisation keep track of them anyway, for example through user feedback, a way to challenge AI outputs, or testing by outsiders? Who is responsible?
How does the organisation weigh AI risks that cannot be measured when deciding to approve, change or stop an AI system? Where is that decision recorded?
How does your organisation collect feedback from the people who use AI systems about how well the AI works in their daily tasks? Where is it recorded?
How does feedback from the people who use your AI systems lead to changes in how you measure AI risk? Can you show a recent change that came from it?
How does your organisation decide which AI risks get treated first and with the most oversight? Who makes these decisions?
How often are priorities and risk limits for AI reviewed, and what triggers an earlier review? Can you show the last one?
For the AI risks you rate as high priority, how does your organisation decide the response (reduce, transfer, avoid or accept)? Who owns each plan?
Where are AI risk responses and system documentation kept, and who can access them?
How does your organisation document the risks that remain after its AI risk controls are in place? Who accepts them?

How do you tell the people who rely on your AI systems (customers, staff, or those who receive them from you) about remaining risks, known limits and safe-use requirements? Where is this communicated?
When your organisation plans to use AI, how does it check that it has the staff, skills and budget to manage the risks? Who decides?
Before choosing an AI system, how do you consider a non-AI or manual alternative, and where is that decision recorded?
How do you use past AI failures and negative impacts to avoid repeating them? Can you show a recent example?
Where your own team lacks the expertise to manage AI risks, how do you bring in outside expertise? Can you show a recent example?

description: AI RMF foundation questions: every question that could be asked once for the organisation (GOVERN and the foundation subcategories of mapping_rules.json), keyed by subcategory, each with the roles it is asked of (none, consumer, producer) and any producer flags. Recorded by record_ai_bank.py questions.
